0.title: Talking with the Living God
0.essay:
Prayer is the breath of the Christian life. It is the moment when the creature turns to the Creator, when the redeemed child speaks to the redeeming Father — not by ritual performance or earned access, but by the right Jesus bought with his blood.

Neglected and longed for

Yet prayer remains one of the most neglected, misunderstood and longed-for practices in the Christian life. We know we should pray more. We feel the distance when we don’t. And we sense, somewhere deep down, that a prayerless life is a self-reliant life — and self-reliance is simply unbelief dressed up as competence.

Relationship before technique

This study does not begin with technique but with relationship. God is not a vending machine, a force to manipulate or a last resort when human resources fail. He is the living God — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — who has drawn near in covenant love, who speaks to us in Scripture, and who invites us to speak to him. Prayer is the conversation at the heart of the covenant, how we live in conscious dependence on the one in whom “we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28).

Every chapter is anchored in Scripture and shaped by the Reformed tradition, with one goal: to help you actually pray — more often, more deeply and with greater joy. It draws on D. A. Carson’s A Call to Spiritual Reformation, Tim Keller’s Prayer, Calvin’s Institutes (book 3, chapter 20), O. Hallesby’s Prayer, E. M. Bounds and the Westminster Shorter Catechism. These voices agree that prayer is both discipline and gift, duty and delight, and that Christ himself is both its ground and its greatest teacher.

The chapters

The Lord’s Prayer — the school of prayer; Intercession — praying for others; Praying the Psalms; Unanswered Prayer — persevering in the dark; Corporate Prayer — the pulse of the church; and Listening Prayer — how God speaks back.

1.title: The Lord’s Prayer: The School of Prayer
1.essay:
When the disciples asked Jesus, “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke 11:1), they were asking the right question of the right person. They had watched him pray — early in the morning, through the night, in Gethsemane — and knew they were seeing something they had never seen.

Pray like this

They were not asking for a formula but for access to what Jesus had. His answer was the Lord’s Prayer: not a liturgy to recite mechanically, but a school to attend daily. “Pray then like this” (Matthew 6:9) — in this shape, in this direction, with these priorities. Prayer that is real, not performed, is contagious; the disciples watched and wanted to learn.

Our Father

The opening words are staggering. That we may call the Creator of the universe “Father”, and mean it, is possible only because Jesus calls him Father and we are in Christ. Reformed theology grounds prayer in adoption. We pray “Our Father” not because God is everyone’s Father by nature, but because “God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Galatians 4:6). The warrant for prayer is not our worthiness or our persistence, but our union with Christ and our adoption into his family. Prayer is trinitarian: “through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:18).

God first

The prayer begins with God — his name, his kingdom, his will — and only then turns to our needs. That order is not accidental; it is teaching. Prayer is first about God’s glory and only then about our need. When every prayer is essentially “fix my life”, prayer has become an extension of self-interest rather than an act of worship.

“Hallowed be your name” asks God himself to act to vindicate and magnify his reputation in the world: “I will vindicate the holiness of my great name” (Ezekiel 36:23). “Your kingdom come” is not a passive wish but an active longing: come, Lord, break in, rule, redeem. “Your will be done” is an act of surrender to which Gethsemane would give its fullest meaning. Before we ask a single thing for ourselves, we have prayed three times that God would be glorified. That is the revolution Jesus works in our prayers.

Bread and forgiveness

The fourth petition is astonishingly ordinary: bread. Not prosperity, not a pain-free life — bread, and daily. Luther said that daily bread includes everything the body needs: food, clothing, shelter, health, good government, peace. To pray for it daily is to confess that we are not self-sufficient.

The fifth links our forgiveness to our forgiving — not as a condition of grace, since we are justified by faith, but as its evidence. Jesus said of the woman who anointed his feet that her love showed how much she had been forgiven, while “he who is forgiven little, loves little” (Luke 7:47). The prayer exposes the heart.

Kept from evil

“And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13) is a prayer of humble self-knowledge. It does not imply that God is the author of temptation (James 1:13–14). It acknowledges that we are weak, that trials expose our frailty, and that we need to be kept. “Evil” may also be read “the evil one”; it is a warfare prayer. We are not strong enough to stand alone against the world, the flesh and the devil. The church has long ended with the doxology found in some manuscripts — “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever” — so that we finish where we began, with God.

How much more

In Luke, Jesus follows the prayer with a parable about persistence and then the greatest promise about prayer in the New Testament: “how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (Luke 11:13). The great gift of prayer is not the answer but the Giver.

What prayer is

The Shorter Catechism asks, “What is prayer?” and answers that it is “an offering up of our desires unto God, for things agreeable to his will, in the name of Christ, with confession of our sins, and thankful acknowledgment of his mercies.” Every phrase carries weight: desires brought honestly, shaped by his will, offered through Christ, with confession and thanks.

Ordered and real

A young father begins every morning by reading the Lord’s Prayer slowly, clause by clause, letting each petition become his own. He is surprised to find that within a month his prayer life has not become mechanical; it has deepened. The structure has given him room to pour out his real self.

A woman who has never prayed aloud is asked to lead her small group in prayer. She follows the shape of the Lord’s Prayer — praise, surrender, petition, confession, trust — and afterwards several people say it was the most moving prayer they have heard in years. She was not eloquent. She was ordered and real.

For reflection

Pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly today, stopping at each petition and letting it open into your own words. How often do your prayers begin with God’s name and kingdom rather than your needs? What does it mean to you to call God “Father”?

2.title: Intercession: Praying for Others
2.essay:
Intercession is perhaps the most selfless form of prayer: placing someone else before God, carrying them into his presence as Aaron carried the names of the tribes on his breastplate. It is the priesthood of all believers made visible in prayer.

We do not pray alone

Jesus himself is the supreme intercessor. “Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). Our prayers rise to God wrapped in his. When we are too weak to pray, when words fail, when we have prayed the same prayer for decades without visible answer, we are still held by the intercession of one who never grows weary and never stops. Always. Every moment. For you. To intercede is to share, however faintly, in his priestly work — not adding to it, but joining it.

And the Spirit helps us. When a situation is too complex, a need too deep, and the words simply will not come, “the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26), according to the will of God. We offer the groaning; the Spirit offers the intercession. That is why prayer is both hard work and a gift.

And God has bound himself by promise to hear his people: “O you who hear prayer, to you shall all flesh come” (Psalm 65:2); “Call to me and I will answer you” (Jeremiah 33:3). Intercession is not a shot in the dark. It is faith aimed at a faithful God.

Paul’s prayer list

Paul’s letters are full of prayers for his churches, and they are worth studying as models. He prays “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you” (Ephesians 1:17–18). He prays for strength in the inner being (Ephesians 3:16–19), “that your love may abound more and more, with knowledge and all discernment” (Philippians 1:9), and for the knowledge of God’s will (Colossians 1:9–12).

What is striking is their content. He rarely prays for relief from circumstances. He prays almost always for spiritual sight, theological rootedness and love. If we took his prayers as our template, our lists would look very different. We would pray less “Lord, solve their problem” and more “Lord, open their eyes to see you in the middle of it.”

A pastor builds a Saturday-morning hour of intercession into his week. He prays for every family in the congregation by name, using Paul’s prayers from Ephesians and Colossians, not only their felt needs. Members begin to notice something different about his preaching. He knows them, he prays for them, and somehow they feel it from the pulpit. Intercession changes the one who prays as much as it serves the one prayed for.

Praying for enemies

“Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Intercession for enemies is the highest form of the practice and the most transforming. It is almost impossible to keep hating someone you are genuinely praying for by name. Jesus commands it not because it is easy but because it reflects the kingdom: the Father “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good” (Matthew 5:45). Many believers have found that sustained prayer for someone who hurt them has, over time, produced a real love they could never have manufactured.

Keeping a list alive

A prayer list can easily become mechanical. Some things help. Pray Scripture over people, especially Paul’s prayers. Pray for a few people each day rather than everyone every day. Note dates and answers, so you can give thanks. And let names come to mind through the day as invitations to pray on the spot.

Not glamorous, but powerful

Intercession happens behind closed doors, often with no visible fruit for years. A mother has prayed for her prodigal son for twenty-three years. Her prayer journal is full of his name, dated entries, scriptures she has claimed and laments she has wept. She has not given up. Augustine’s mother Monica prayed for her wayward son for years, and a bishop told her that the son of so many tears could not be lost (Confessions 3.12). It is among the most powerful things a believer can do.

For reflection

Whom has God placed on your heart to carry before him? Rewrite your prayer list using Ephesians 1:17–19 or Philippians 1:9–11. Is there someone who has hurt you whom you could begin praying for by name? How does Hebrews 7:25 encourage you when your prayers feel weak?

3.title: Praying the Psalms: The Prayer Book of the Church
3.essay:
Athanasius compared the Psalms to a mirror in which we see our own souls, and Dietrich Bonhoeffer called his short study of them The Prayer Book of the Bible. The church has always returned to the Psalms because they do something no other part of Scripture does so directly: they model prayer.

Every register

The Psalms are not instructions about prayer; they are prayer, in every register: ecstatic praise (Psalm 150), utter desolation (Psalm 88), confident trust (Psalm 23), bewildered lament (Psalm 73), honest confession (Psalm 51), even terrible cries for judgment (Psalm 109). They give us permission to bring our whole selves to God. Calvin called them “an anatomy of all the parts of the soul”.

They cure two diseases of modern prayer. Sentimentality limits prayer to warm, assured feelings; the Psalms teach us to pray in darkness, doubt, anger and grief. Shallowness keeps prayer at the surface of need; the Psalms drive us into theology, history, covenant and hope. To pray through them regularly is to be taught to pray by the Holy Spirit himself, who breathed them out.

Faith in the dark

“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1). Jesus prayed this from the cross (Matthew 27:46), so the cry of desolation is not a failure of faith. It is the prayer of the Son of God in his darkest hour. That is the most important thing to know about the laments: they are prayers of the faithful in extremity. The psalmist does not simply declare, “You have forsaken me.” He asks why — which presupposes a God who is there, who has purposes and who can be questioned. Lament is faith speaking from the darkness.

A woman in a season of unexplained depression finds Psalm 88, the darkest of the Psalms, which ends without resolution: “my companions have become darkness” (Psalm 88:18). For the first time in months she feels that the Bible understands her. She prays it aloud and weeps. Something loosens. She has not been given answers, but she has been given company in the dark.

Confession that seeks holiness

Psalm 51 is David’s prayer after Nathan confronted him about Bathsheba and Uriah. “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions” (Psalm 51:1). It names sin specifically and appeals to God’s character rather than its own. And it asks for more than pardon: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10). Confession that aims only at relief, not holiness, has misunderstood grace.

Until I went into the sanctuary

Psalm 73 is the prayer of someone whose faith was nearly shipwrecked by the prosperity of the wicked: “But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled” (Psalm 73:2). The turning point comes in verses 16–17: “But when I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end.” The shift was not first intellectual but a matter of where he went. In worship God reordered his vision. That is why gathered worship is not optional for the struggling Christian. Among God’s people, perspective is restored.

Everything that has breath

The Psalter ends in pure praise: “Let everything that has breath praise the LORD!” (Psalm 150:6). That is where all prayer is heading. Lament moves toward praise; confession moves toward praise; intercession is praise that believes God can act. Even the darkest psalms are addressed to a God worth addressing, and that address is itself praise. All of life is moving toward the moment when every voice cries, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain” (Revelation 5:12). The Psalms are our rehearsal.

Praying with Jesus

Bonhoeffer’s insight is decisive: the Psalms are the prayers of Jesus before they are ours. He is the true Israel and the perfect worshipper, who prayed Psalm 22 on the cross and whose resurrection fulfilled Psalm 16 (Acts 2:25–28). We pray the Psalms through him and with him. That is why we can pray the laments without despair: Christ has been there ahead of us, and he has come through.

The Reformed tradition has always given the Psalms a privileged place in worship — the Genevan and Scottish Psalters, and in some churches the singing of psalms alone — because they are God-given words with which to address God. One pastor began each Sunday service by praying a psalm together with the congregation, a different one each week. After a year, elders reported that their own prayers had deepened and their vocabulary had grown, and several members had begun praying the Psalms at home.

How to start

Read a psalm slowly. Notice what kind it is — praise, lament, confession, thanksgiving, trust, wisdom, kingship. Then pray it: turn its words into your own, line by line, bringing your life into its shape. Many find it helpful to pray through the whole Psalter regularly, perhaps five psalms a day for a month.

For reflection

Which kind of psalm do you most need right now — lament, confession, trust or praise? Pray Psalm 13 or Psalm 51 aloud this week. How does it change your praying to know that Jesus prayed the Psalms before you?

4.title: Unanswered Prayer: Persevering in the Dark
4.essay:
Few things test faith more sharply than unanswered prayer. You have prayed faithfully and persistently, and the answer has not come. The cancer remains. The marriage did not survive. The prodigal is still far from home. The depression has not lifted.

Three false conclusions

The temptation is to one of three conclusions: God does not exist; God does not care; or something is wrong with me that has blocked my prayers. Each is false, but in the dark each feels overwhelmingly real. Scripture does not explain the experience away. It honours it.

How long?

“How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1). The church has prayed that cry for millennia. And Psalm 13 is the grammar of persevering prayer in four movements: lament (“How long?”), petition (“Consider and answer me, O LORD my God”), trust (“But I have trusted in your steadfast love”) and praise (“I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me”, Psalm 13:5–6). It does not explain why God has hidden his face, or resolve the tension intellectually. But it moves, from “How long?” to “I will sing”, and that movement is an act of faith. The psalmist has not received the answer, but he has decided that God is still trustworthy. That decision, made in the dark, is the heart of persevering prayer.

Do not lose heart

Jesus told the parable of the persistent widow “to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). If an unjust judge yields to persistence, “will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night?” (Luke 18:7). The danger in unanswered prayer is not that we ask too boldly but that we give up too soon. Persistence is spiritual courage, a refusal to believe that silence means absence. God’s delays are not his denials.

Paul’s thorn

Paul pleaded three times for the removal of his thorn in the flesh — recalling Jesus’ three prayers in Gethsemane — and God said no. But he said something better: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Paul leaves the thorn unspecified, perhaps pastorally, so that every reader can supply their own. And notice the tense: grace is sufficient, now, in this weakness. The answer was not healing but presence. Sometimes that is the greater gift.

Gethsemane

The supreme unanswered prayer in history was prayed in a garden: “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). The Son prayed with tears and agony, and the cup was not taken away. The Father said no to the Son. And through that unanswered prayer came the redemption of the world. We will never know, this side of glory, what is being accomplished through prayers that seem unanswered. But we know that “he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” will “graciously give us all things” (Romans 8:32), and that he is working, even in silence, for our good and his glory.

Sovereign, good and wise

So prayer is not first about outcomes but about relationship. The God who says “no”, or “wait”, or “I am doing something you cannot yet see” is the same God who says, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). God’s sovereignty comforts us in unanswered prayer only when it is held together with his goodness and wisdom. He is sovereign: “Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases” (Psalm 115:3). He is good: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17). He is wise: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). Held together, they turn unanswered prayer from a sign of God’s absence into a door to trust: he knows what we do not and sees what we cannot. God always answers prayer, but sometimes the answer is no, because he loves us too much to give us everything we ask.

Not resignation but hope

Joni Eareckson Tada has prayed for physical healing for over fifty years and is still in a wheelchair. She has said again and again that she is grateful: that her suffering has produced a depth of faith, a ministry of comfort to millions and a longing for heaven she would not trade. That is not resignation but resurrection faith. The unanswered prayer has carried something greater than the answer would have.

A father prays for his son’s salvation for thirty years. The son comes to faith on his deathbed — but he comes. The prayer was answered, only not on the father’s timetable.

For reflection

Which unanswered prayer is hardest for you right now? Pray it through the four movements of Psalm 13. Which of the three false conclusions are you most tempted by, and how does Gethsemane answer it? What would it mean to keep praying and “not lose heart”?

5.title: Corporate Prayer: The Pulse of the Church
5.essay:
The early church was a praying church. “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42). “The prayers” suggests regular, shared times of prayer, kept with intention.

A praying church

“Devoted themselves” is a strong word: to persist in, to attend to constantly. The early church was not casual about any of its four pillars. Prayer was not a private supplement to public worship but one of the defining practices of the gathered body. A church that loses any of the four has lost something essential.

Before Pentecost, about a hundred and twenty believers “with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer” (Acts 1:14), and the Spirit fell on a praying community. The history of revival is the history of corporate prayer.

Earnest prayer

When Herod imprisoned Peter, “earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church” (Acts 12:5). The word means stretched out, strained, intense. They were fighting for Peter’s life with their prayers. The answer came so dramatically that when Peter knocked, the servant girl Rhoda, in her joy, ran to tell the others and left him standing outside the gate (Acts 12:14). A church that prays together expects God to act, and is sometimes astonished when he does.

First of all

“First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:1–2). “First of all” sets the priority: before anything else in the gathering, prayer. And its scope is enormous — all people, rulers and everyone in authority. The church’s prayer is not only for the comfort of its members but a ministry to the world. When it prays for rulers it disagrees with, cities that oppose the gospel and people who are hostile, it acts as a kingdom of priests interceding for the world God so loves.

Two or three

“For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them” (Matthew 18:20). In context Jesus is speaking of the church acting together in discipline, but the promise of his presence holds for his gathered people as they pray. It is not magic but relationship. Gathered in his name — his character, authority and purposes, not our own agendas — we have his presence. The promise is not about church size but about the power of the smallest community gathered in faith. A prayer meeting of three in Christ’s name is a sacred thing.

God is not absent in private prayer. But there is a corporate dimension of prayer that private practice cannot replace. The body prays as a body. The Westminster Directory for Public Worship (1645) gave careful guidance on the content of public prayer, recognising that how the church prays shapes what it believes — lex orandi, lex credendi, the law of prayer is the law of belief.

The weakest hour

Yet corporate prayer is often the weakest hour of the evangelical church’s week. The prayer meeting is poorly attended, the prayers perfunctory or repetitive, and few sense that anything of consequence is happening. That is a crisis — not because attending a prayer meeting is a virtue in itself, but because thin corporate prayer reflects and reinforces a thin experience of God’s presence and power in the church’s life.

The answer is not more programmes. It is recovering prayer as a means of grace: the living conversation of the body of Christ with its Head. Rich corporate prayer is varied and participatory. It mixes praise, confession, thanksgiving and intercession; it prays Scripture; it lets many voices take part briefly rather than a few at length; it prays specifically for the church, the city, the persecuted and the nations; and it gives thanks when answers come.

Concerts of prayer

When revival came to Northampton in 1734, Jonathan Edwards reported that the whole town seemed seized with concern for the things of God. Years later, having seen what God can do, he urged churches everywhere to join in a “concert of prayer” — agreed seasons of united prayer across many congregations for the spread of the gospel (An Humble Attempt, 1747). Those concerts of prayer helped prepare the way for the revivals and missionary movement that followed.

Today the church in Korea is known around the world for its early-morning prayer meetings, some gathering thousands before dawn. The fruit in church growth, missionary sending and spiritual vitality has been remarkable. Corporate prayer is not the only means of grace, but it may be the most neglected in the Western church. The goal is not more prayer meetings, but the kind of prayer that changes the room, and then changes the world.

For reflection

How strong is corporate prayer in your church? What would “earnest prayer” look like for a need your church faces now? Could you gather two or three others to pray regularly? Whom should your church be praying for “first of all”?

6.title: Listening Prayer: How God Speaks Back
6.essay:
Prayer is a conversation, not a monologue. If we speak to God but never listen for him, we have turned prayer into something less than a relationship. Yet “listening prayer” is also one of the most misunderstood, and sometimes misused, ideas in Christian spirituality.

The questions

How does God speak? Through an audible voice? A feeling? A Scripture that leaps off the page? A sense of peace? A word from another believer? And how do we tell God’s voice from our own desires, or from the enemy’s counterfeits? The Reformed tradition is careful here, and the caution is warranted.

God has spoken in his Son

“Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2). The supreme word of God is Jesus Christ. Everything God said through prophets, visions and dreams reaches its completion in the Word made flesh. To listen to God is finally to listen to Jesus — in the Gospels, in the whole Scripture that points to him, and through the Spirit who glorifies him (John 16:14).

So the primary, normative and sufficient way God speaks to his people is Scripture, illuminated by the Spirit (2 Timothy 3:16–17). The canon is closed; no new revelation is needed or expected. The Westminster Confession says that “the whole counsel of God, concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man’s salvation, faith and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture.”

The Spirit speaks through the word

Yet within that framework the Spirit is alive and active. He brings particular scriptures to mind at particular moments, creates deep impressions of peace or conviction, speaks through the body of Christ, and works through a conscience shaped by the word. The Confession speaks of “the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our hearts.” The Spirit does not speak around Scripture or beyond it, but through it and by it, and that speaking is personal, specific and alive. Prayer is how truth about God moves from the head to the heart, and meditation is the listening half of that movement.

So impressions must be tested by the word. A sense of leading that contradicts Scripture is not from the Spirit. Impressions that fit Scripture are best held humbly, weighed with wise counsel, and treated as wisdom rather than as a new word from God.

My sheep hear my voice

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27). This is not a promise of audible revelation or private prophecy, but of relational knowing. Sheep recognise the shepherd’s voice because they know him; they have been with him, listened to him and learned his ways. Our ability to “hear” God grows with the depth of our relationship with him in his word. A new believer and a seasoned saint hear the same Shepherd, but the saint has learned to recognise his voice through a lifetime of intimacy with Scripture. Listening prayer is cultivated, not conjured.

Be still

“Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). The word means let go, release, stop striving. Psalm 46 describes cosmic upheaval — mountains tumbling into the sea, nations raging — and in the middle of it calls us to stop trying to control what only God can manage, and in the quiet to know that he is God. Stillness in prayer is not a technique for mystical experience but an act of theological surrender. I am not God; he is. Let me stop talking long enough to remember it. The stillness is not emptiness but attentiveness.

A low whisper

Elijah, burned out and longing to die, met God not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in “the sound of a low whisper” (1 Kings 19:12) — the older translations’ “still small voice”. That is often the pattern. God seldom speaks in the spectacular. He speaks in the quiet, to those who have stopped performing long enough to listen. Elijah passed through wind, earthquake and fire before he heard the whisper. Sometimes fasting, solitude and silence are the passage through the noise to the place where God whispers. The whisper is worth the journey.

Listen first, then speak

George Müller, who cared for over ten thousand orphans in Bristol, began each day with Scripture and meditation before he prayed. He said he needed to fill his mind with God’s word before he could pray in line with God’s will. The discipline transformed his prayer. He could pray more specifically, confidently and peacefully, because his listening shaped his speaking. That is listening prayer at its most practical, and it is open to every believer every morning: read slowly, notice what God is saying in the text, and then pray it back to him.

For reflection

Do you give God time to “speak” through his word before you speak to him? How would you test an impression or sense of leading? What noise in your life makes stillness hard? Try Müller’s pattern tomorrow: read, meditate, then pray what you have read.
